PLaCA: Learning Patch-Level Future Latent Change for Action Generation

Zhan Yi Affiliation: School of Robotics and Automation, Nanjing University    Yuchen Wang Affiliation: Suzhou, Jiangsu, China    Chao Li Affiliation: njuyizhan@smail.nju.edu.cn, wyc_nju@smail.nju.edu.cn, lichao_nju@smail.nju.edu.cn,    Lei Hong Affiliation: leihong@smail.nju.edu.cn, yby@nju.edu.cn    Boyuan Yang* Affiliation: *Corresponding author.
Abstract

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating how the environment will change. Existing world-action models explore future image prediction and latent dynamics modeling. However, generating complete future images can be computationally expensive, while highly compressed latent representations may obscure local changes. To address these challenges, we propose PLaCA, a world-to-action framework built around future latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially structured patch-level future latent change from the current multimodal input, preserving local information about expected environmental changes. We introduce patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize regions undergoing larger changes and a future-to-action interface that explicitly incorporates predicted future latent change into action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Long show that PLaCA achieves a 79.0% success rate, improving upon the Action-only baseline by 5.0 percentage points. On CALVIN, PLaCA improves the average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564. These improvements are achieved while updating only 2.95% of the model parameters during the second training stage, demonstrating the effectiveness of future latent change modeling for downstream robotic manipulation.

1 Introduction

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models typically generate robot actions from current visual observations and language instructions [7, 15, 30]. However, in manipulation tasks such as grasping, pushing, and placing, effective action generation requires more than understanding the current environment. A policy must also consider how its actions may change object positions, contact relations, and local environmental states. To incorporate such future information, recent studies have explored integrating world modeling with VLA policies, motivating the development of world-action modeling (WAM)  [10, 40].

Existing approaches represent future information in different ways. Some predict future images or videos [8, 55], while others model future states or temporal dynamics in latent space [16, 2]. Recent studies have further explored compact latent motion representations [29, 46, 47]. Latent-space modeling has become a widely adopted approach in world modeling and robot learning [16, 2, 46]. While pixel-level future prediction provides rich visual details, generating complete future images often involves reconstructing substantial redundant visual content, leading to additional computational costs [44, 46]. In contrast, latent-space modeling avoids explicit pixel-level reconstruction, yet choosing an appropriate future representation for robotic manipulation remains an important question. For action generation, it may not be necessary to recover the complete future state or all intermediate dynamics. Instead, a policy may benefit from information about how the environment is expected to change.

Recent work has shown that differences between latent states can capture information related to robot motion. StaMo [29] learns highly compressed latent state representations and uses the latent displacement between states to represent robot motion. It also explores latent motion prediction for world modeling. However, latent representations differ in how they preserve spatial information. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), when a robot places an object into a box, the changes are mainly concentrated around the robot arm and the object, while much of the background remains unchanged. Highly compressed state representations can encode such changes, but they do not explicitly preserve the correspondence between spatial locations and their latent changes. In contrast, retaining the patch-level spatial structure allows future changes at different image locations to be represented separately, as shown in Fig. 1(b). Moreover, the magnitude of future change can vary considerably across patches, while uniform patch supervision does not specifically emphasize regions undergoing larger changes. This motivates our first research question: How can we preserve the spatial structure of future latent change and learn local changes more effectively by accounting for their different magnitudes?

Another important question is how future modeling can be effectively coupled with action generation. Prior work has explored different approaches, including jointly learning future prediction and action policies within shared architectures [40, 46], using predicted future images or video plans to guide downstream control [52, 14], and leveraging learned latent or interaction dynamics for action inference [37, 41]. These studies provide different ways of using future information to inform robotic behavior. For the spatially structured future latent change considered in this work, the predicted representation preserves local information about expected environmental changes across image regions. This motivates investigating how such spatially organized predictions can be incorporated into action representations to support action generation. We therefore pose our second research question: How can predicted future latent change be effectively used to support action generation?

To address these questions, we propose PLaCA, a world-to-action framework built around future latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially structured patch-level future latent change from the current multimodal input and employs patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize regions with larger changes. We further introduce a future-to-action interface that incorporates the predicted future latent change into the action representation, allowing it to directly contribute to full action-chunk generation.

We evaluate PLaCA on LIBERO-Long, achieving a 79.0% task success rate. Ablation studies demonstrate that preserving fine-grained spatial structure, employing change-aware supervision, and incorporating predicted future latent change into action generation through the future-to-action interface contribute to improved downstream manipulation success rates.

Our main contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We investigate patch-level future latent change modeling, which directly predicts future latent change from the current multimodal input while preserving its spatial structure, providing local future information for action generation.

  • •

    We propose patch-level change-aware supervision, which adjusts the supervision weights according to the magnitude of ground-truth future latent change. Ablation results show that this approach improves closed-loop manipulation performance compared with uniform patch supervision.

  • •

    We design an explicit future-to-action interface that incorporates the final predicted future latent change into the action representation, allowing future information to directly contribute to full action-chunk generation.

2 Related Work

2.1 World-Action Modeling

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models unify visual observations, language instructions, and robot actions within end-to-end policies, extending large-scale vision-language models toward general-purpose robotic control [57, 25, 6, 7, 12, 15, 30]. While conventional VLAs primarily focus on predicting continuous actions or action sequences from current multimodal observations [22, 5, 38, 43, 42], recent studies have increasingly incorporated future modeling, enabling policies to reason not only about what to do but also about what may happen after an action is executed [10, 56, 52, 14]. This trend has gradually extended VLA research from direct observation-to-action mapping toward joint modeling of environmental dynamics and robot behavior.

One line of work models future environmental changes through image or video prediction [44], while other approaches jointly learn future modeling and action generation [10, 56]. WorldAgen performs future-state prediction and action prediction within a unified Transformer, allowing world modeling and policy learning to share internal representations [40]. CoT-VLA uses predicted future images as intermediate visual guidance for subsequent action generation [52]. DynBridge learns interaction dynamics that connect future interaction modeling with robot control [41], while Motus further integrates latent action modeling, world modeling, and action generation into a unified framework, using shared latent representations to characterize the relationship between robot behavior and environmental changes [4]. DreamVLA combines dynamic-region-guided future information with spatial and semantic cues for action generation [51], while Mantis learns latent visual foresight with a separate prediction head [48]. Collectively, these studies reflect a growing trend in which future modeling is increasingly coupled with action generation through shared or explicitly connected representations. We focus on directly predicting spatially structured future latent change and incorporating its predicted tokens into the action representation through gated cross-attention.

2.2 Latent Dynamics

Future image and video prediction provides a detailed description of environmental changes, but generating full future frames can be computationally expensive [55, 8]. Recent studies have therefore explored latent state, latent motion, and latent action representations for future modeling and robot control [9] [49, 3, 2, 16].

One line of work focuses on representing dynamics in latent space. CoWVLA separates structural and motion information and learns a continuous latent motion chain to represent temporal evolution [46]. CoMo learns continuous latent motion by combining temporal differences with contrastive learning [47]. StaMo takes a different approach by learning highly compressed latent state representations from individual observations. It shows that differences between these states contain robot motion information and can support action decoding. StaMo further uses state and motion representations as prediction targets for VLA world modeling and explores latent-motion co-training [29]. These studies explore different ways to capture temporal changes in latent space, including continuous motion representations and differences between compact latent states.

Another line of work investigates how latent dynamics can support action generation. VideoWorld learns discrete latent codes that represent future visual changes and uses the predicted codes together with visual information for inverse dynamics-based action decoding [37]. Latent Bridge instead predicts continuous feature changes to update latent representations, allowing the policy to reduce repeated VLM computation during action generation [31]. These approaches illustrate different ways of using learned latent dynamics to support action generation.

Our work focuses on learning spatially structured future latent change and using the predicted representation for action generation.

3 Method

3.1 Overview

We consider robotic manipulation conditioned on multimodal context. At time step tt, the current observation is Ot={Otc}c=1CO_{t}=\{O_{t}^{c}\}_{c=1}^{C}, where CC is the number of camera views. The language instruction, robot state, and available observation-action history are denoted by ℓ\ell, sts_{t}, and ℋt\mathcal{H}_{t}, respectively. Together, they form the multimodal input 𝒳t=(Ot,ℓ,st,ℋt)\mathcal{X}_{t}=(O_{t},\ell,s_{t},\mathcal{H}_{t}). Our goal is to predict a full action chunk At={at,…,at+H−1}∈ℝH×daA_{t}=\{a_{t},\ldots,a_{t+H-1}\}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d_{a}}, where HH is the action horizon and dad_{a} is the action dimension [53, 11, 24]. We use H=3H=3 and set the future prediction horizon to Δ=3\Delta=3, aligning the future observation with the state reached after executing the action chunk.

As shown in Fig. 2, our framework consists of a shared multimodal backbone, a future-change decoder, and a future-to-action interface. The shared backbone ℬθ\mathcal{B}_{\theta} processes the multimodal input together with action-query tokens QaQ^{a} to obtain an initial action representation Ht(0)H_{t}^{(0)} [39, 45]. A residual adapter produces the shared action-query representation [42, 19]:

Ht(0)\displaystyle H_{t}^{(0)} =ℬθ​(𝒳t,Qa),\displaystyle=\mathcal{B}_{\theta}(\mathcal{X}_{t},Q^{a}), (1)
Hta\displaystyle H_{t}^{a} =Ht(0)+α​Adapter⁡(Ht(0)),\displaystyle=H_{t}^{(0)}+\alpha\,\operatorname{Adapter}(H_{t}^{(0)}),

where α\alpha is a zero-initialized learnable scalar. The same representation HtaH_{t}^{a} is used for future latent change prediction and action generation.

The overall prediction process is formulated as

Δ​Z^t\displaystyle\widehat{\Delta Z}_{t} =𝒟f​(Qf,Hta),\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}_{f}(Q^{f},H_{t}^{a}), (2)
H~ta\displaystyle\widetilde{H}_{t}^{a} =ℱϕ​(Hta,Δ​Z^t),\displaystyle=\mathcal{F}_{\phi}(H_{t}^{a},\widehat{\Delta Z}_{t}),
A^t\displaystyle\widehat{A}_{t} =𝒟a​(H~ta),\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}_{a}(\widetilde{H}_{t}^{a}),

where 𝒟f\mathcal{D}_{f} denotes the future-change decoder, QfQ^{f} denotes learnable change queries, ℱϕ\mathcal{F}_{\phi} is the future-to-action interface, and 𝒟a\mathcal{D}_{a} is the action decoder. The predicted future latent change Δ​Z^t\widehat{\Delta Z}_{t} provides both a future prediction target during training and conditioning information for action generation.

3.2 Patch-Level Future Latent Change Modeling

We model future information as changes between the current and future latent states while preserving their patch-level spatial structure. Instead of representing the change using a single global feature, we predict a separate latent change vector for each patch location in every camera view.

Ground-Truth Future Latent Change. As illustrated in Fig. 3(a), we construct the ground-truth future latent change from the current observation OtO_{t} and future observation Ot+ΔO_{t+\Delta}. A frozen visual encoder EvisE_{\mathrm{vis}} extracts patch-level latent state representations  [13, 17]. For the pp-th patch of camera view cc, we define :

ztc,p\displaystyle z_{t}^{c,p} =Evis​(Otc)p,\displaystyle=E_{\mathrm{vis}}(O_{t}^{c})_{p}, (3)
zt+Δc,p\displaystyle z_{t+\Delta}^{c,p} =Evis​(Ot+Δc)p,\displaystyle=E_{\mathrm{vis}}(O_{t+\Delta}^{c})_{p},
Δ​zt∗,c,p\displaystyle\Delta z_{t}^{*,c,p} =zt+Δc,p−ztc,p.\displaystyle=z_{t+\Delta}^{c,p}-z_{t}^{c,p}.

Collecting the differences across all camera views and patch locations yields Δ​Zt∗∈ℝC×P×dz\Delta Z_{t}^{*}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times P\times d_{z}}, where P=Hp​WpP=H_{p}W_{p} denotes the number of patches per view, HpH_{p} and WpW_{p} are the height and width of the patch grid, and dzd_{z} is the latent feature dimension.

We use a frozen MAE ViT encoder [17, 13] to construct these targets. Unlike the compact visual tokens supplied to the policy backbone, the supervision targets retain the complete patch grid without spatial pooling. Each difference is computed between features at the same image patch location, preserving the spatial organization of the latent representation.

Future Latent Change Prediction. To predict this representation, we introduce Qf∈ℝ(C​P)×dQ^{f}\in\mathbb{R}^{(CP)\times d} as learnable change queries, with each query assigned to a camera view and patch location. Here, dd denotes the hidden dimension of the future-change decoder. A Transformer-based future-change decoder uses these queries [39, 23] to attend to the shared action-query representation HtaH_{t}^{a}, aggregating information from the current multimodal context.

The decoder outputs are projected into the visual latent space to obtain

Δ​Z^t=𝒟f​(Qf,Hta)∈ℝC×P×dz.\widehat{\Delta Z}_{t}=\mathcal{D}_{f}(Q^{f},H_{t}^{a})\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times P\times d_{z}}. (4)

The predicted vectors retain their camera and patch indices and are supervised at the corresponding spatial locations. Importantly, the decoder directly predicts the continuous future latent change rather than first reconstructing a future latent state. This prediction is subsequently used by the future-to-action interface.

3.3 Patch-Level Change-Aware Supervision

Future latent change is generally distributed unevenly across image regions. While some patches undergo substantial changes, others remain relatively stable over the prediction horizon. To account for these differences, we introduce patch-level change-aware supervision that assigns larger relative weights to patches with greater ground-truth changes. Figure 3(b) illustrates how patch-wise change magnitudes are used to determine the supervision weights.

For each patch, we measure its change magnitude as rc,p=‖Δ​zt∗,c,p‖2r_{c,p}=\|\Delta z_{t}^{*,c,p}\|_{2} and compute the mean magnitude within each sample:

r¯=1C​P​∑c,prc,p.\bar{r}=\frac{1}{CP}\sum_{c,p}r_{c,p}. (5)

We then construct normalized supervision weights:

w~c,p\displaystyle\widetilde{w}_{c,p} =clip⁡(1+η⁡(rc,pmax⁡(r¯,ϵ)−1),wmin,wmax),\displaystyle=\operatorname{clip}\left(1+\eta\left(\frac{r_{c,p}}{\max(\bar{r},\epsilon)}-1\right),w_{\min},w_{\max}\right), (6)
wc,p\displaystyle w_{c,p} =w~c,pmax⁡(1C​P​∑c′,p′w~c′,p′,ϵ).\displaystyle=\frac{\widetilde{w}_{c,p}}{\max\left(\frac{1}{CP}\sum_{c^{\prime},p^{\prime}}\widetilde{w}_{c^{\prime},p^{\prime}},\epsilon\right)}.

Here, η\eta controls the strength of change-aware weighting. We use η=0.75\eta=0.75, wmin=0.25w_{\min}=0.25, and wmax=4w_{\max}=4, with ϵ=10−8\epsilon=10^{-8} for numerical stability. The weights are normalized after clipping to maintain a mean of one. All patches remain supervised, including those with small changes.

We combine a SmoothL1 regression loss with a cosine directional loss to supervise the predicted future latent change. For each patch, these are defined as

ℓregc,p\displaystyle\ell_{\mathrm{reg}}^{c,p} =1dz​∑j=1dzSmoothL1⁡(Δ​z^t,jc,p,Δ​zt,j∗,c,p),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{d_{z}}\sum_{j=1}^{d_{z}}\operatorname{SmoothL1}\left(\widehat{\Delta z}_{t,j}^{c,p},\Delta z_{t,j}^{*,c,p}\right), (7)
ℓdirc,p\displaystyle\ell_{\mathrm{dir}}^{c,p} =1−cos⁡(Δ​z^tc,p,Δ​zt∗,c,p),\displaystyle=1-\operatorname{cos}\left(\widehat{\Delta z}_{t}^{c,p},\Delta z_{t}^{*,c,p}\right),

where cosine similarity is computed with numerically stabilized vector norms. The weighted future latent change objective is

ℒchange=1C​P​∑c,pwc,p​(ℓregc,p+λdir​ℓdirc,p),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{change}}=\frac{1}{CP}\sum_{c,p}w_{c,p}\left(\ell_{\mathrm{reg}}^{c,p}+\lambda_{\mathrm{dir}}\ell_{\mathrm{dir}}^{c,p}\right), (8)

where λdir=0.2\lambda_{\mathrm{dir}}=0.2. As illustrated in Fig. 3(c), the patch-wise weights adjust the contributions of the regression and directional losses. These weights are used only during training and are not required during inference.

3.4 Future-to-Action Interface

Predicting future latent change provides information about the expected environmental changes. To make this information available to the action-generation pathway, we introduce a future-to-action interface that conditions the action representation on the predicted patch-level future latent change.

Future-Change Conditioning. We use the final predicted change vectors Δ​Z^t\widehat{\Delta Z}_{t}, rather than the hidden features of the future-change decoder, as the input to the interface. After flattening the camera and patch dimensions, a learnable projection 𝒫ϕ\mathcal{P}_{\phi} maps the predicted change into the action feature space:

Ft=𝒫ϕ​(Δ​Z^t)∈ℝ(C​P)×d.F_{t}=\mathcal{P}_{\phi}\left(\widehat{\Delta Z}_{t}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{(CP)\times d}. (9)

We then use cross-attention to incorporate the predicted future latent change into the action representation [39, 1]. The shared action-query representation HtaH_{t}^{a} serves as the Query, while FtF_{t} serves as the Key and Value:

Ut=LN⁡(MHA⁡(Q=Hta,K=Ft,V=Ft)).U_{t}=\operatorname{LN}\left(\operatorname{MHA}\left(Q=H_{t}^{a},\,K=F_{t},\,V=F_{t}\right)\right). (10)

This allows each action query to aggregate information from the predicted patch-level future latent change.

Gated Residual Integration. To control the contribution of predicted future information, we employ a learnable scalar gate β\beta and update the action representation through residual fusion [1]:

H~ta\displaystyle\widetilde{H}_{t}^{a} =Hta+β​Ut,\displaystyle=H_{t}^{a}+\beta U_{t}, (11)
A^t\displaystyle\widehat{A}_{t} =𝒟a​(H~ta).\displaystyle=\mathcal{D}_{a}(\widetilde{H}_{t}^{a}).

The gate β\beta is initialized to zero and learned jointly with the other trainable modules. It is independent of the residual-adapter coefficient α\alpha in Eq. (1).

The resulting action representation is decoded into the full action chunk. Thus, the predicted future latent change contributes directly to action generation through a separate conditioning pathway, rather than serving only as an auxiliary prediction target.

3.5 Joint Learning and Initialization

We adopt a two-stage training strategy. First, we train an action-only policy using behavioral cloning [53, 11, 32] to establish an observation-to-action mapping. We then initialize the joint model from this policy and introduce the future-change decoder and future-to-action interface. During the second stage, the visual and language encoders and the original backbone weights remain frozen, while lightweight backbone adapters, future-modeling modules, the interface, and action-generation modules are optimized.

Action Generation Objective. We supervise the predicted full action chunk using SmoothL1 loss for arm actions and binary cross-entropy for gripper states:

ℒaction=ℒarmSmoothL1+λg​ℒgripperBCE,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{arm}}^{\mathrm{SmoothL1}}+\lambda_{g}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{gripper}}^{\mathrm{BCE}}, (12)

where λg\lambda_{g} controls the contribution of the gripper loss.

Training samples contain two consecutive action chunks [53, 34] associated with observation endpoints O0O_{0}, O3O_{3}, and O6O_{6}. Predicted future latent change from both chunks is incorporated into their respective action representations. Both chunks receive action supervision, while direct future latent change supervision is applied to the latest chunk, which corresponds to the action chunk executed during closed-loop inference. Specifically, we use Δ​Z3∗=Evis​(O6)−Evis​(O3)\Delta Z_{3}^{*}=E_{\mathrm{vis}}(O_{6})-E_{\mathrm{vis}}(O_{3}) as the prediction target.

Joint Optimization. The complete second-stage training objective is

ℒtotal=ℒaction+λchange​ℒchange,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{total}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{action}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{change}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{change}}, (13)

where λchange\lambda_{\mathrm{change}} controls the contribution of future latent change supervision.

The future-change decoder receives direct supervision from ℒchange\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{change}}. Because its predictions are incorporated into the action-generation pathway without detachment, the action objective can also update the future-change decoder as the gate β\beta learns a nonzero value. During inference, the model predicts future latent change and generates the full action chunk using only the available multimodal context, without access to future observations.

4 Experiments

We evaluate PLaCA on two robotic manipulation benchmarks, LIBERO-Long and CALVIN, and compare its performance with representative methods. We further conduct ablation studies to examine the contributions of patch-level spatial structure, change-aware supervision, and the future-to-action interface.

4.1 Experimental Setup

Benchmarks and Datasets. LIBERO-Long [28, 24, 35] consists of 10 long-horizon manipulation tasks. We use 50 expert demonstrations per task, totaling 500 trajectories, with 450 for training and 50 for validation. All variants share the same trajectory-level split. Each task is evaluated with 20 closed-loop rollouts, yielding 200 episodes per model.

CALVIN [33] evaluates long-horizon language-conditioned robotic manipulation across different environments. We adopt the ABC→\rightarrowD setting, training on environments A, B, and C and evaluating on the unseen environment D. We evaluate 1,000 task sequences, each containing five consecutive subtasks, and report the Average Sequence Length (ASL).

Implementation Details. We build PLaCA on a Qwen-based Transformer backbone [45, 39] with frozen MAE visual and CLIP language encoders [17, 36]. Following the two-stage training procedure described in Sec. 3, all future-modeling variants are initialized from the same Action-only checkpoint. During the second stage, the pretrained backbone weights remain frozen, with rank-8 LoRA [19] applied to the last six Transformer layers. The future-change decoder, future-to-action interface, and action-generation modules are jointly optimized.

4.2 Evaluation on Simulation Benchmarks

Results on LIBERO-Long. We evaluate PLaCA on the LIBERO-Long benchmark, which consists of 10 long-horizon manipulation tasks involving object grasping and placement, container manipulation, and multi-stage task execution. We evaluate all 10 tasks with 20 closed-loop rollouts per task, resulting in 200 episodes in total. We report the average task success rate.

As shown in Table 1, PLaCA achieves a success rate of 79.0% on LIBERO-Long, outperforming the reported results of several representative methods, including Dita, ThinkAct, MolmoAct,and PDF, while achieving performance comparable to Fast-ThinkAct (79.4%). Notably, PLaCA contains only 394.83M parameters, of which 11.66M (2.95%) are trainable during the second training stage. By directly predicting spatially structured future latent change and using it for action generation, PLaCA incorporates future information without generating complete future images or intermediate motion sequences. This design provides a practical way to incorporate future modeling within a relatively small model, achieving competitive closed-loop performance with a limited number of trainable parameters.

Compared with the Action-only policy built on the same base architecture, PLaCA improves the average success rate from 74.0% to 79.0%, a gain of 5.0 percentage points. The contributions of individual components are further examined through ablation studies in Sec. 4.3.

Per-Task Performance. To examine the performance across different manipulation tasks, Fig. 4 compares the per-task success rates of the Action-only policy and PLaCA on all 10 LIBERO-Long tasks.

PLaCA improves the success rate on 8 of the 10 tasks and maintains the same performance on the remaining two tasks. In particular, PLaCA achieves a 100% success rate on Tasks 1 and 3. However, Task 8, which requires placing two moka pots on the stove, remains challenging, with a success rate of 20%.

Results on CALVIN. To further assess PLaCA on sequential robotic manipulation, we evaluate its performance on CALVIN under the ABC→\rightarrowD setting. As shown in Table 2, PLaCA achieves an ASL of 3.564, outperforming the Action-only baseline (2.784) by 0.780. This result demonstrates that PLaCA also improves sequential task execution in an unseen environment.

4.3 Ablation Studies

We conduct ablation studies on LIBERO-Long to examine three key designs in PLaCA: patch-level future latent change modeling, patch-level change-aware supervision, and the future-to-action interface. All variants are evaluated on the same 10 tasks with 20 closed-loop rollouts per task. The results are summarized in Table 3.

Effect of Additional Training. To examine whether performance gains arise from additional training, we continue training the Action-only policy for 40 epochs from the same checkpoint, matching the second-stage training duration of PLaCA. The extended Action-only baseline achieves 72.5%, compared with 74.0% for the original baseline and 79.0% for PLaCA. This indicates that the improvement is attributable to future latent change modeling rather than additional training alone.

Patch-Level Future Latent Change Modeling. We examine this design from two perspectives: the prediction target and spatial structure. First, we replace future latent change with absolute future latent as the prediction target, while retaining the same future-to-action interface and training configuration. Directly predicting absolute future latent achieves 74.5%, 4.5 percentage points below PLaCA (79.0%), demonstrating the benefit of explicitly modeling future latent change.

Second, we investigate spatial structure by varying the patch grid resolution, preserving patch-wise representations and supervision rather than removing them altogether. Reducing the grid from 14×1414\times 14 to 7×77\times 7 decreases the success rate from 79.0% to 77.5%, suggesting that retaining richer local spatial change information benefits action generation.

Effect of Patch-Level Change-Aware Supervision. Replacing change-aware supervision with uniform patch weighting reduces the success rate from 79.0% to 76.0%. This demonstrates the benefit of adjusting supervision weights according to local future latent change magnitudes, enabling more effective learning of future environmental changes.

Effect of the Future-to-Action Interface. Using future latent change prediction only as an auxiliary training objective achieves 76.5%. Explicitly incorporating the predicted future latent change into action generation through the future-to-action interface improves the success rate to 79.0%, confirming the effectiveness of directly coupling future modeling with action generation.

5 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose PLaCA, a world-to-action framework built around future latent change, aiming to make future modeling more directly contribute to robot action generation. By preserving fine-grained spatial structure, employing change-aware supervision, and explicitly incorporating predicted future latent change into action generation, PLaCA establishes a direct connection between future modeling and action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and CALVIN demonstrate improved downstream manipulation performance, while ablation studies further validate the effectiveness of the proposed designs. Notably, PLaCA achieves performance improvements by updating only a small fraction of model parameters during the second training stage, suggesting that future modeling can effectively enhance action generation with limited parameter updates. Overall, our results highlight spatially structured future latent change as an effective representation for connecting future modeling with robot action generation.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
